CausalChain: Chronic liver disease and tumor burden → impaired hepatocyte synthetic and excretory capacity → lower albumin production and higher bilirubin levels (worsened ALBI grade) → emergence of a pro-inflammatory and immunomodulatory hepatic microenvironment → altered immune cell recruitment and function (e.g., antigen presentation, T-cell activation) → modulation of both efficacy and hepatotoxicity of immune checkpoint inhibitors
Hypothesis: Dynamic alterations in the ALBI grade actively influence the hepatic immune microenvironment in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma, thereby modulating their response and toxicity to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapies.
Abstract: We propose that fluctuations in the albumin‐bilirubin (ALBI) grade are not only passive reflections of liver functional reserve but also actively shape the hepatic immune microenvironment, thereby modulating the response to immunotherapies in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Specifically, the reduced albumin synthesis and increased bilirubin levels associated with a worsening ALBI grade may promote a pro‐inflammatory milieu and alter immune cell recruitment and activation within the tumor microenvironment. These changes can influence both the efficacy and toxicity profile of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). This hypothesis suggests that early dynamic changes in ALBI grade during treatment could serve as both a prognostic biomarker and a mechanistic mediator in immunotherapy outcomes in HCC.
